problem_solved: Kazakhstan rural districts had acute radiologist and pathologist shortages — 70% of districts had no specialist radiology interpretation services, creating 3-6 week delays for chest X-ray and CT readings. AI diagnostic assistance for tuberculosis (high-burden country), pneumonia, and chest oncology screening would reduce diagnostic backlog and enable remote screening at district polyclinics without full-time radiologist presence.
architecture_summary: Cloud-deployed AI diagnostic platform integrated into Kazakhstan national EPSD (Electronic Population State Database) health system. Three AI modules: (1) Chest X-ray TB/pneumonia screening — convolutional neural network trained on 250,000+ KZ radiological images, calibrated to local TB strain prevalence; (2) CT lung nodule detection — classification of nodule characteristics for oncology referral; (3) ECG interpretation — automated arrhythmia detection for district-level GPs. API integration with district polyclinic PACS (Picture Archiving and Communication Systems). Results streamed to remote radiologist for confirmation. Local cloud hosting at NIT data centres in Nur-Sultan.
outcome_metrics: Deployed in 40+ district polyclinics by 2023. Chest X-ray reading turnaround: from 2 weeks to 4 hours. TB detection sensitivity: 94% (vs 82% for unaided district GP). 12,000+ scans processed monthly. TB case detection increase in screened districts: +23% year-over-year. Radiologist shortage mitigation: 40 districts previously with no radiology interpretation now have AI-first interpretation.
failure_modes: Image quality from district-level X-ray equipment highly variable — some old Soviet-era machines produced images outside training distribution causing AI underperformance. Integration with legacy PACS systems required custom connectors for each equipment brand. Clinician trust took 9 months to develop — initial resistance to AI recommendations from senior specialists.
replicability_factors: Kazakhstan TB epidemiology similar to UZ and KG. Soviet-era X-ray equipment installed base is similar across CIS. Damumed actively deploying in UZ (pilot reported 2023) and seeking broader CA expansion. NIT advisory support available. Budget is achievable at sub-$5M for UZ/KG pilot scale.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ TB burden is among the highest in CIS (18,000+ new cases/year). District polyclinic X-ray shortage is identical to KZ pattern. Damumed is ALREADY in UZ pilot as of 2023. Ministry of Health e-prescription decree (ПП-415, 2023) creates procurement pathway. Most directly actionable health AI case in the entire tournament. Budget: $3-6M for national rollout on existing health infrastructure. Donor pathway: World Bank Health project, WHO, Global Fund.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG TB burden is severe (Kyrgyzstan has highest TB rate in CIS per WHO). District polyclinic infrastructure is sparse, X-ray quality is variable. Damumed's KZ architecture directly applicable. Budget at KG scale: $1.5-3M. Donor pathway: Global Fund (TB programme), WHO, ADB health projects. KG Ministry of Health already in dialogue with AI health vendors per ADB project documents.
key_adaptation_required: Uzbek/Kyrgyz language interface for clinicians. Training data augmentation with local X-ray image sets (equipment variation). Integration with national health e-platform (UZ E-Health, KG e-health registry). WHO TB detection sensitivity threshold compliance validation.

problem_solved: India's 1.4 billion population faced a massive urban-rural healthcare divide — rural areas had 1 doctor per 10,000 population vs WHO standard of 1 per 1,000. Specialist consultations required expensive multi-day travel. eSanjeevani created a national telemedicine platform allowing rural patients to access specialists at district, state, and national levels via video consultation, integrated with national health ID and EMR systems.
architecture_summary: Government-built (C-DAC and MoHFW) web + mobile telemedicine platform. Two modes: (1) HWC (Health and Wellness Centre) to hospital hub-and-spoke — rural HWC staff initiate consultation on patient's behalf to district/state specialists; (2) OPD (Outpatient) direct patient access via mobile app. Integration with Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission health ID, national drug formulary, e-prescription standards (HL7 FHIR). Video calls via WebRTC. AI triage module added 2022: symptom-based pre-consultation questionnaire routes patient to appropriate specialty. Hosted on NIC Government Cloud.
outcome_metrics: By 2023: 175M+ consultations delivered (largest telemedicine platform in world by volume). 100,000+ registered doctors. 25,000+ HWC centres using the platform. Maternal mortality reduction: 18% in districts with high eSanjeevani adoption. COVID-era usage peak: 700,000 consultations/day. Average wait time: 12 minutes. 28 states integrated.
failure_modes: Video quality issues in low-bandwidth rural areas required fallback to audio-only mode (reducing clinical utility). Rural patients without smartphones required HWC mediation — direct-to-patient model has lower adoption in poorest districts. EMR integration incomplete in 30% of states. Doctor registration attrition: 35% of registered doctors had <5 consultations in first year.
replicability_factors: C-DAC open-sourced core eSanjeevani platform. WHO references as global telemedicine case study. ASEAN health ministers briefed. Architecture documented in Health Affairs and WHO publications. Scalable from district pilot to national deployment.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ faces exact same urban-rural healthcare divide — Tashkent concentration of specialists vs Ferghana/Karakalpakstan district shortages. eSanjeevani hub-and-spoke model maps to UZ district polyclinic (poliklinika) → tuman → viloyat → national hierarchy. UZ E-Health platform (ПП-415) provides the integration foundation. Cost: $3-5M national telemedicine deployment leveraging open-source eSanjeevani code. Donor pathway: World Bank Health, ADB, KOICA.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG has the most severe urban-rural health divide in the dataset: Bishkek has specialists, Issyk-Kul/Naryn/Batken have near-zero specialists. eSanjeevani's small-budget ($15M) for massive scale is compelling for KG. Adaptation: Russian/Kyrgyz language interface, integration with MHIF (Mandatory Health Insurance Fund) billing. Donor pathway: WHO, World Bank, ADB, AKDN (rural connectivity).
key_adaptation_required: Russian and Uzbek/Kyrgyz language interface. Integration with national health IDs (UZ E-Health ID, KG health registration). Adaptation of AI triage module for disease burden profiles (TB, cardiovascular, maternal health are different in CA vs India). Connectivity backup for video degradation (audio-only fallback already proven in India).

problem_solved: Estonia's fragmented health IT systems — each hospital had separate EHR systems with no interoperability — meant patient histories were invisible to treating physicians outside the originating hospital, creating duplicate tests, adverse drug interactions, and care gaps. A national digital health record platform was needed to aggregate patient data from all care providers and make it accessible to authorised clinicians and patients.
architecture_summary: TEHIK (Health and Welfare Information Systems Centre) operates the national e-Health system: Patient Portal (patsiendoportaal.ee) for citizen access, Clinical Portal for clinicians, X-Road integration connecting all hospitals and GP practices, and central data repositories (e-prescription, digital registration, laboratory results, radiological images). All data access logged and auditable — patients can see who accessed their records. e-Prescription: 99% of prescriptions electronic since 2010. FHIR-based API layer added 2021 for modern app integrations.
outcome_metrics: 99% of prescriptions electronic. 100% of hospitals connected. Average GP time per patient reduced 12 minutes (pre-filled history, no manual record requests). Adverse drug interaction alerts: 180,000+ clinical warnings/year. Duplicate lab test reduction: 22%. Patients access records 1.2M+ times/year. Estonia ranked global top-5 for e-Health systems.
failure_modes: Latvia eHealth copycat attempt (cautionary): Estonia's system cost Latvia 3x the original budget and took 4 restarts over 10 years (see case-lv-ehealth). Integration with private clinics initially required mandate legislation. Data quality inconsistency when rural GPs entered records manually. Initial clinician adoption needed incentive payments (2008-2012).
replicability_factors: TEHIK provides advisory services internationally. Architecture documented in HIMSS publications. EU co-funded regional health data exchange (HealthData@EU) provides further bilateral. Key lesson: X-Road as integration backbone eliminates need for centralised health database.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ is building E-Health platform under ПП-415 (2023). Estonia's architecture — X-Road integration of existing hospital systems, central data repository, e-prescription — is the blueprint. Key lesson to embed in UZ implementation: incentivise GP adoption with fee-for-digital-services payments in early years. Patient portal adds political visibility (citizens see their records). Budget: $8-15M for UZ national E-Health at Estonian-equivalent scope. World Bank Health project donor pathway.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG has a fragmented health IT landscape similar to Estonia in 2008. Key constraint: KG hospital systems include some Russian-made software (МИС, old Soviet-era systems). X-Road (Tunduk) is already the integration layer. TEHIK advisory could deploy KG national e-Health in 3-5 years. Budget: $5-8M leveraging existing Tunduk infrastructure. Donor pathway: World Bank, ADB, AKDN.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Uzbek/Kyrgyz clinical interface for patient portal and clinician portal. Integration with Soviet-era МИС systems (requires custom connectors). Audit access log requirement (legally mandated in Estonia — needs equivalent KG/UZ personal data law provision). Incentive payments for GP adoption in early phases.

sources.title: TEHIK — Health and Welfare Information Systems Centre

problem_solved: Latvia attempted to replicate Estonia's e-Health success. Similar problem statement: fragmented hospital IT, paper prescriptions, no national patient record. Latvia had access to Estonia's architecture blueprints and shared X-Road integration layer. Should have been a straightforward replication — it became a 13-year saga of failed procurements and restarts.
architecture_summary: Programme attempted: centralised national health portal, e-prescription system, EHR integration via eVeseliba portal. Reality: three complete procurement failures (2009, 2014, 2018). Final 2020 restart used more modular approach: e-prescription only first (live 2021), patient portal second (partial live 2022). Total systems: Tieto (Finnish vendor) won 2020 tender for e-prescription, NIC Latvia (in-house) built patient portal. X-Road integration was available but agencies refused to connect.
outcome_metrics: NEGATIVE across first 3 attempts. Fourth attempt: e-prescription live 2021 (partial adoption). Patient portal: partial functionality 2022. Total spend: €72M+ for equivalent of what Estonia built for €25M in half the time. Latvia's per-capita cost: 10x Estonia. Adoption rate in 2023: 40% of prescriptions electronic (vs Estonia 99%).
failure_modes: SYSTEMIC: Each procurement chose large international vendors (IBM, Accenture) who over-engineered solutions and failed delivery. Scope kept expanding mid-procurement. Hospital sector stakeholders sabotaged integration to protect existing vendor relationships. Government changed 4 times during implementation, creating priority discontinuity. e-Health designated as 'critical infrastructure' prevented agile iteration. No dedicated implementation unit (cf. TEHIK in Estonia).
replicability_factors: This is the ESSENTIAL cautionary case for UZ E-Health and KG health platform. The failure pattern: large international vendor, over-scoped procurement, no dedicated implementation unit, hospital sector resistance, government change discontinuity.
uz_transferability_rationale: Score 2 = CAUTIONARY CASE. UZ E-Health must avoid the Latvia pattern. Specific risks for UZ: (1) over-scoped initial procurement (build everything at once); (2) no TEHIK-equivalent implementation unit with technical authority; (3) international vendor promises without local capacity building; (4) hospital sector resistance from existing software vendors (multiple Russian МИС vendors are embedded in UZ hospitals). UZ must adopt Estonia's modular approach: e-prescription FIRST, patient portal SECOND.
kg_transferability_rationale: Same cautionary rating. KG additionally at risk due to smaller government IT capacity. Key protection: ensure Tunduk (GP Infocom) has mandate as the integration hub, avoiding the Latvia problem of agencies refusing to connect. Scope strictly to e-prescription + basic EHR in Phase 1.
key_adaptation_required: N/A — CAUTIONARY. Lessons: (1) build dedicated implementation unit first (cf. TEHIK); (2) procure modularly — one service at a time; (3) mandate hospital connection via regulation, not just incentives; (4) phase approach: e-prescription → patient portal → full EHR.

problem_solved: Bangladesh had 14,000+ Union Digital Centres (UDCs) connecting 130M+ rural citizens to government services, but health services required physical travel to district hospitals. The a2i (Access to Information) programme under the Prime Minister's Office piloted telemedicine service at UDCs — placing videoconference-enabled health consultation in rural community centres already trusted by local populations.
architecture_summary: Low-cost hub-and-spoke: each UDC equipped with laptop, broadband (3G fallback), and simple vitals equipment (thermometer, BP cuff, pulse oximeter). District hospital provides scheduled telemedicine sessions. Village-level para-doctor (trained local resident) facilitates consultation, inputs vitals, translates for specialist. Digital prescription generated and printed at UDC. DGDA (Directorate General of Drug Administration) maintained drug database for prescription validation. USAID and UNDP co-financed. No complex EHR initially — simplified Google-Forms-based consultation recording.
outcome_metrics: By 2018: 500+ UDC telemedicine points. 2M+ consultations delivered. Travel cost savings: average BDT 800 ($8) per patient per consultation. Maternal health visits: 30% increase in covered districts. GP referral accuracy improved when UDC para-doctor present. Government scaled programme nationally under Shasthya Seva Kendra initiative.
failure_modes: Para-doctor training quality highly variable — some centres had untrained operators undermining clinical quality. Broadband reliability in flash-flood zones: significant outages during monsoon season. Doctor participation dependent on voluntary overtime — not sustainable without payment model. Google Forms-based recording not interoperable with any hospital EHR system.
replicability_factors: a2i published full implementation methodology. UNDP replicated in several ASEAN and Africa countries. Bangladesh's use of existing UDC infrastructure (no new buildings needed) is the key insight for UZ mahalla network and KG ayil aymak.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ has 14,000+ mahalla (neighborhood) offices as existing touchpoints. Deploying telemedicine at mahalla level — leveraging existing community trust infrastructure rather than building new health centres — is the Bangladesh lesson. UZ MoH could run a 200-mahalla pilot in Ferghana Valley for $1-2M. Donor pathway: World Bank Health, ADB, AKDN. Key adaptation: Uzbek-language UI, integration with UZ E-Health not Google Forms.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG's network of ayil aymak (rural commune) offices provides the same infrastructure as Bangladesh UDCs. Kyrgyz telemedicine from Bishkek National Hospital to Naryn/Talas provinces is the target. AKDN rural connectivity projects create donor-infrastructure alignment. $1-3M pilot deployment at 100 rural ayil aymak centres is achievable. USAID-successor and UNDP both active in KG health.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Kyrgyz language clinical interface. Para-doctor/feldcher role definition (KG has feldcher tradition that maps directly to Bangladesh para-doctor). Connectivity via satellite (AKDN Sky/Starlink hybrid) for most remote areas. Payment model for specialist telemedicine time.

problem_solved: Rwanda Ministry of Health needed to extend primary healthcare access to rural populations with 1 doctor per 6,700 citizens. Babyl (later rebranded as Aluna Health) deployed an AI-powered symptom checker and triage chatbot accessible via feature phones (USSD) and smartphones, directing patients to appropriate care level — self-care, community health worker, clinic, or hospital emergency.
architecture_summary: Multi-channel clinical AI: USSD (feature phone, no data plan required), WhatsApp, web, and app. Clinical AI: validated symptom-checking decision tree augmented with ML triage model trained on 100,000+ consultations in Rwanda. Nurse call-back service integrated for medium-risk cases. Integration with Rwanda health insurance (RSSB) for subsidised consultations. Appointment booking for clinic visits. Backend: AWS with Rwanda data residency agreement. Regulatory approval: Rwanda FDA cleared AI as Class II medical device.
outcome_metrics: By 2021: 2.7M registered users (25% of Rwanda's adult population). 1M+ consultations delivered. USSD access: 45% of users via feature phone. 30% reduction in unnecessary emergency room visits in Kigali pilot districts. Rwanda Health Minister awarded WHO Director-General Award for AI health innovation. Clinical accuracy: 87% triage accuracy vs senior GP benchmark.
failure_modes: Commercially unsustainable without government subsidy — $3/consultation cost vs Rwanda per-capita health spend of $50/year. Rwanda government ended contract renewal due to budget constraints in 2022. Clinical AI performed poorly on rare diseases and complex multi-morbidity. French/Kinyarwanda language barriers (Babyl built primarily in English).
replicability_factors: Babyl/Aluna has deployed in 7 countries. USSD-first approach (no smartphone required) is the key innovation for low-income populations. WHO published Rwanda Babyl as case study. USAID and Gates Foundation funded expansion documentation.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ smartphone penetration is 65% — USSD fallback not as critical as Rwanda but still relevant for rural Karakalpakstan. AI triage chatbot in Russian + Uzbek for EPIGU integration is the target application. Key lesson: government subsidy model is essential for sustainability; commercial model won't work. MoH could integrate as a feature in existing EPIGU app. Budget: $2-4M deployment leveraging existing EPIGU infrastructure.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG smartphone penetration is 70% but rural Batken/Osh have feature phone populations. USSD-based health triage is directly relevant. Russian + Kyrgyz language triage chatbot via WhatsApp or USSD is technically feasible in 12 months. MHIF (Mandatory Health Insurance Fund) integration for subsidised consultations is the business model. Donor pathway: USAID-successor, WHO.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Uzbek/Kyrgyz language clinical AI. Training data calibration for CA disease burden (TB, cardiovascular, maternal). USSD integration with major telecoms (Ucell, UMS for UZ; MegaCom, O!/Nur Telecom for KG). MHIF billing integration for sustainability.

case_name: India Aarogya Setu + CoWIN Health Platform
problem_solved: India needed national health ID, COVID contact tracing, and vaccine certificate infrastructure simultaneously during the pandemic. CoWIN became the world's largest vaccine management platform: citizen registration, appointment booking, dose tracking, and certificate issuance for 2.2 billion doses administered. The certificate infrastructure later extended to all health events under Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), creating a universal health ID backbone.
architecture_summary: Three-component stack: (1) CoWIN — open-source vaccine management (beneficiary registration, slot booking, dose tracking, digital certificate generation); (2) Aarogya Setu — contact tracing app using Bluetooth + GPS; (3) ABDM — universal health ID linking CoWIN, eSanjeevani, and hospital EHRs. CoWIN architecture: microservices on NIC GovCloud, ABHA (Ayushman Bharat Health Account) as the universal health ID, FHIR-based health records, verifiable credentials (W3C VC standard) for certificates. Open-sourced by India under DPI (Digital Public Infrastructure) framework; deployed in 50+ countries.
outcome_metrics: 2.2 billion doses managed on CoWIN. 700M+ ABHA health IDs created. 30+ countries requested CoWIN source code. Digital vaccine certificates recognised by 150+ countries. ABDM: 250M+ linked health records by 2023. G20 India Presidency proposed CoWIN as global DPI standard.
failure_modes: Aarogya Setu contact tracing: civil society criticism of data retention (12 months), mandatory installation requirements, and surveillance risk. Aarogya Setu data breach allegation (2020) — government disputed but trust damaged. CoWIN registration excluded elderly citizens without smartphones — 30M+ vaccinated via paper registers. Rural connectivity caused appointment slot losses (sessions expired before upload).
replicability_factors: CoWIN open-sourced under India's DPI programme. WHO endorsement for multilateral deployment. SCO countries explicitly studying India DPI. UZ and KG are SCO members and have received Indian advisory delegation for digital health ID. Budget for fork and deploy: $2-4M.
uz_transferability_rationale: UZ E-Health platform (ПП-415) needs a universal health ID layer — ABHA/CoWIN architecture is the cost-effective foundation. UZ is SCO member with active India DPI dialogue. ABDM's FHIR-based approach maps to international health data standards. Key: CoWIN is free to fork and deploy. Donor pathway: India-bilateral technical assistance, World Bank Digital Development, WHO. Budget: $3-5M for UZ national health ID deployment.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG can fork CoWIN for its mandatory vaccination registry (already maintained by MoH). ABHA health ID concept — linking all health events across the lifecycle — is the right architectural direction for KG's fragmented health record landscape. Donor pathway: WHO, India bilateral, World Bank. Cost: $1.5-2.5M for KG-scale deployment.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Kyrgyz language interface. Offline-first mode for connectivity gaps (India solved this — patterns exist). Integration with MHIF (KG health insurance) billing. Personal data law alignment for health data retention.

case_name: Kazakhstan EPSD Electronic Health Record System
problem_solved: Kazakhstan had 17+ regional health MIS systems with no interoperability, preventing care coordination across regional boundaries. National statistics were manually aggregated with 6-month delays, preventing effective disease surveillance. A national Electronic Population State Database (EPSD) health module was needed to provide real-time patient data access across all regions.
architecture_summary: National Health Information System built by NIT Kazakhstan: Patient Registration System (PRS) as central identifier, Electronic Medical Record (EMR) aggregated from regional MIS via FHIR-based API gateway. Key module: Digital Polyclinic tracking GP visits, referrals, and chronic disease management. Integration with OSMS (compulsory health insurance) for billing. E-prescription: integrated with national drug registry and pharmacy POS systems. Telemedicine added 2021. AI layer: predictive analytics for disease burden forecasting added 2022.
outcome_metrics: By 2023: 100% of polyclinics connected. 17M Kazakhstani health records digitised. E-prescription coverage: 80% of prescriptions. Real-time disease surveillance: MOH receives daily regional epidemiological data. COVID response enabled real-time tracking. Healthcare cost reduction: estimated 15% from duplicate test elimination.
failure_modes: Regional MIS integration required custom connectors for 7 different legacy systems — 3 years and $12M overrun. Physician resistance to EMR data entry ('second shift' syndrome) required workflow redesign incentives. Private hospital sector integration delayed 4 years. Data quality audits showed 25% of legacy migrated records had errors requiring manual correction.
replicability_factors: NIT has deployed KZ EPSD advisory missions to neighbouring CIS countries. Architecture is documented in World Bank CA health sector reports. Russian-language clinical workflow maps directly to UZ and KG.
uz_transferability_rationale: KZ EPSD is the direct reference for UZ E-Health (ПП-415). Regional MIS integration lessons — particularly the connector strategy for legacy systems — are directly applicable given UZ's similar mix of Soviet-era and modern hospital software. E-prescription integration with pharmacy POS is the Phase 1 module UZ should replicate. Budget: KZ spent $55M over 7 years; UZ could achieve equivalent in 4 years for $20-30M leveraging KZ architecture. NIT advisory available.
kg_transferability_rationale: KG health system scale is 1/3 of KZ. EPSD architecture principles directly applicable. Key: GP-level EMR integration (Digital Polyclinic equivalent) is the highest-impact module for KG's primary care. Budget at KG scale: $8-15M. NIT advisory could accelerate by 2 years vs building from scratch.
key_adaptation_required: Russian/Uzbek/Kyrgyz clinical interfaces. KG-specific insurance integration (MHIF billing codes differ from KZ OSMS). Naryn/Talas offline mode for connectivity-challenged polyclinics. Adaptation of KZ e-prescription format to KZ drug formulary differences vs UZ/KG.
